answer: An agent economy can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may vote on payments, then slash that stake when an independent audit proves coordinated fraud. Splitting into a garden of fake agents does not multiply influence for free: every identity ties up capital, and a sparrow-sized account still risks losing its deposit. The nebula of identities an attacker needs to control therefore raises the upfront cost and makes detection financially painful, though it cannot stop a wealthy attacker outright.
